newsitem.title: USA: Texas Senate panel okays bill against lurid lyrics.
newsitem.headline: Texas Senate panel okays bill against lurid lyrics.

text.p: Companies promoting song lyrics involving violence and sexual acts such as necrophilia may have to change their tune if they want to see any state investment money from Texas.

Under a bill approved Thursday by the state Senate Finance Committee, Texas entities charged with investing state funds would be banned from investing in companies directly associated with offensive lyrics as well as the those indirectly associated by virtue of a 10 percent or more stake in such enterprises.
The full senate is expected to vote on the measure next week.

The bill defines such lyrics as those depicting acts of criminal violence including murder and assault; necrophilia, beastiality or pedophilia; illegal use of controlled substances; crimininal street gang activity; degradation or denigration of females; or violence against a particular sex, race or ethnic group.

The bill also would require a governmental entity or retirement system that currently owns such investments to divest "as soon as is reasonable and practical considering protection of capital, but no later than Jan. 1, 1999."

Republican State Sen. Bill Ratliff, chairman of the finance committee and the bill's author, said it stemmed from an article he read earlier this year quoting Dr. C DeLores Tucker, national chairwoman of the National Political Congress of Black Women Inc.
The article discussed such lyrics' effects on children. Tucker sent Ratliff samples of the lyrics, and he distributed them to some fellow committee members who shared his "horror" at them.

In February, Texas' Permanent School Fund announced plans to sell $3.5 million of Seagram Co. stock after state lawmakers' objections to lyrics on recordings marketed by Seagram subsidiary, MCA, according to a report in the May 1997 issue of Fiscal Notes, a publication from Texas Comptroller John Sharp's office said.
Comment could not be obtained from a Seagram's spokeswoman Friday.
